summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a desktop application that combines a computational model with interactive 3D visualization. It uses NASA LOLA and NASA/JPL SPICE data to assess how local terrain affects sunlight and Earth visibility.

Users can choose a location themselves or use existing presets, set mission dates and duration, adjust lander-related settings, and explore conditions in an interactive 3D viewport. The application estimates Earth visibility, sunlight availability, darkness duration, and the power generated by the lander’s solar panel using a simplified model. It also identifies favorable periods when Earth is visible and sunlight is available at the same time. Saved mission configurations can be compared to find the most favorable option.

The project brings NASA datasets together in a practical planning environment, helping users explore how location and timing affect conditions for lunar surface missions.
details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator lets users explore how conditions at a lunar landing site change throughout a mission. We wanted to bring terrain, sunlight, and Earth visibility into one workspace so users could see how these factors relate to each other.

 

Users choose a location under "Landing site", enter Latitude / Longitude, or click directly on the Moon. "Date and duration" sets the mission timeframe. "Lander hardware" includes "Mast height" (height above the surface used for visibility calculations), "Earth clearance" (additional angular margin required for Earth visibility), and "Panel rating (W)" (nominal solar-panel power). "Orbit view", "Lander", and "Region" provide different perspectives of the selected location.

 

The computational model combines NASA LOLA elevation data with Sun and Earth positions prepared using NASA/JPL SPICE. It samples the surrounding terrain to calculate the local horizon, accounting for lunar curvature and Mast height. Visibility depends on whether the Sun and Earth are above this horizon, with Earth clearance additionally applied to Earth.

 

"Solar and power" shows estimated output, Sunset, Availability, Longest night, and Sun elevation. "Earth communication" shows whether Earth is "Visible" or "Blocked", together with Earthset, Availability, Joint window, and Earth elevation. Availability statistics use hourly samples, while power estimates account for solar elevation and terrain obstruction.

 

The Mission timeline contains "Sunlight", "Earth link", and "Favorable window" tracks. The last track highlights periods when sunlight and Earth visibility overlap. Users can drag the cursor or press "Play" to explore changing conditions.

 

"Save" stores a location and its settings, while "Restore" opens the saved history. "Compare sites" shows sunlight and Earth visibility, favorable hours, longest darkness, mean solar power, and estimated energy. Saved configurations retain their own settings, so matching dates and parameters should be used for equivalent comparisons.

 

We developed the application using Qt Design Studio, Qt 6, QML, JavaScript, Qt Quick 3D, and a C++ launcher. Python and SpiceyPy were used for scientific data preparation. The lander and selection pin models were created in Blender, while the lunar globe and local terrain geometry were generated programmatically using NASA elevation data. Bundled datasets allow the application to work offline.

 

Our creative approach connects scientific calculations directly to an interactive 3D environment. Users can select a location, inspect its terrain, and compare mission conditions without switching between separate tools.

 

We considered performance, readability, data resolution, and model limitations. Global terrain spacing is approximately 474m at the equator, with 80m data in the bundled south-polar coverage. The model cannot establish landing safety or guarantee a radio link, and power estimates exclude batteries, thermal effects, and electrical losses.

 

The project supports preliminary mission planning and education by helping users understand how location and timing affect lighting, power-generation opportunities, and Earth visibility.
